title: Understanding Pocket Park Accessibility Through Pedestrian Infrastructure and Microclimatic Conditions
content: Pocket parks can provide important recreational and environmental benefits in dense urban areas, but their effectiveness depends on whether residents can reach them safely and comfortably. This study examines pedestrian accessibility to Hayy Al Ain Park in Al Mabela, Muscat, Oman, focusing on three dimensions: street connectivity, physical infrastructural barriers, and microclimatic constraints. A bilingual questionnaire using a five-point Likert scale was administered to 43 respondents, and the relationships among the study constructs were assessed using SmartPLS with bootstrapping. Although 69.8% of respondents lived within a 5–10-minute walk of the park, 34.9% reported visiting it rarely and 25.6% never visited. Respondents also reported limited sidewalk continuity, indirect or inconvenient routes, inadequate shade, and heat exposure as important  barriers to walking. The structural model explained 32.7% of the variance in pocket park accessibility. Microclimatic Constraints showed the strongest relationship with accessibility and were the only statistically significant predictor, whereas Street Connectivity and Physical Infrastructural Barriers were not statistically significant. The findings suggest that proximity alone is insufficient for evaluating pocket park accessibility and highlight the importance of integrating pedestrian infrastructure and climate-responsive street design with neighborhood green-space planning.
